title: Example
body_md:
The well-known Auslander-Reiten formula 
\[
 D_{\mathbf{J}}\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}_{\Lambda}(A,B) \simeq \overline{\operatorname{\mathrm{Hom}}}_{\Lambda} (B, D_{\mathbf{J}}\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A),
 \]  
is a basic tool in Auslander-Reiten theory. Here  $\Lambda$ is an algebra over a commutative ring $\Bbbk$ (which could be $\mathbb{Z}$), $A$ and $B$ are (left) $\Lambda$-modules, $A$ is finitely presented, $\mathbf{J}$ is an injective $\Bbbk$-module, $D_{\mathbf{J}} := \operatorname{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\Bbbk}(\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} , \mathbf{J})$, and the transpose is computed using any finite presentation of $A$. The overlined $\operatorname{\mathrm{Hom}}$ on the right-hand side stands for $\operatorname{\mathrm{Hom}}$ modulo injectives, i.e., the quotient of the usual $\operatorname{\mathrm{Hom}}$ by the subgroup of all maps factoring through injectives. It ``neutralizes'' the projective ambiguity in the definition of the transpose, which is turned into an injective ambiguity 
by~$D_{\mathbf{J}}$. If~$A$ is not finitely presented, then  the left-hand side still makes sense, but the right-hand side is not well-defined. This may happen even when $A$ is finitely presented but the transpose is computed via an infinite presentation. In fact, this may happen even for $A \simeq 0$. To see that, assume that $\Lambda$ is not left-coherent. Then, by a theorem of Chase~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{Chase}, 
$\Lambda_{\Lambda}^{N}$ is not flat for some $N$. Now choose the following  projective resolution of the zero module
\[
0 \longrightarrow \prescript{}{\Lambda}\Lambda^{(N)} \overset{\mathrm{id}}\longrightarrow \prescript{}{\Lambda}\Lambda^{(N)} \longrightarrow 0 \longrightarrow 0 \longrightarrow 0.
\]
Computing the transpose with this resolution, we have $\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A \simeq \Lambda_{\Lambda}^{N}$. Now choose $\Bbbk : = \mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbf{J} := \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$. By a theorem of Lambek~\cite[p.~238]{L64}, the character module $D_{\mathbf{J}}\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A$ is not injective. Evaluating the right-hand side of the formula on $B := D_{\mathbf{J}}\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A$
we have a nonzero group, whereas the left-hand side is zero. Thus the formula fails.

label: Eq:bidual
title: Example
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $A$ and $B$ be left $\Lambda$-modules. Next we examine the canonical map 
\[
\varphi : A^{\ast} \otimes B \longrightarrow (A, B) : (f, b) \mapsto \big(a \mapsto f(a)b\big).
\]
As $B$ is canonically isomorphic to $(\Lambda, B)$, we interpret $\varphi$ as the map 
\[
(A, \Lambda) \otimes (\Lambda, B) \to (A,B)
\]
given by the ``composition" of the arguments. Therefore the image of 
$\varphi$ consists of all maps $A \to B$ factoring through finitely generated projectives.

Under the assumption that $A$ is finitely presented, we have an exact sequence of functors~\cite[Proposition~7.1]{A66}.
\begin{equation}\label{D:tor}
\xymatrix@R1pt@C15pt
	{
	0 \ar[r]
	& \operatorname{\mathrm{Tor}}_{2}(\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]
	& A^{\ast} \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \ar[r]^{\lambda_{A}}
	& (A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]
	& \operatorname{\mathrm{Tor}}_{1}(\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]
	& 0.
	}\footnote{The reader may check that $\lambda_{A}$ is the zeroth left-derived transformation for $(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$.}
\end{equation}

However, when $A$ is not finitely generated, this sequence fails to be exact already for vector spaces over a field. In that case, the end terms vanish, and the exactness of the sequence would force $\lambda_{A}$ to be an isomorphism, which is impossible since, evaluating it on $B : = A$, we would have the identity map on $A$ factor through a finite-dimensional vector space, a contradiction.

title: Definition
body_md: We shall call~\eqref{D:rfs-co-fun} the right fundamental sequence of $F$.

body_md: Obvious.

label: T:co-fund-right
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) The claim that~~\eqref{D:rfs-co-fun} is a complex is easily checked by a diagram chase of arrows (with or without elements) in~\eqref{D:circ-diag-extended} and is left to the reader as an exercise. 

For the exactness claim, we have to show the exactness at the first two terms of each row. For the first row, this is true by the definition of the injective stabilization. 

For the second row, since $\kappa_{1}$ is monic, it is easy to check that the fragment of~\eqref{D:rfs-co} connecting $R^{0}F$ and $R^{1}F$ is part of the circular sequence of the triangle $F(I^{0}), F(\Sigma B), Z_{1}$ in the diagram~\eqref{D:circ-diag-extended}, and we are done by the exactness of the circular sequence. 

For the third row, since $\kappa_{2}$ is monic, we have the fragment 
\[
Z_{1} \longrightarrow \overline{F}(\Sigma^{2} B) \longrightarrow S^{1}F(\Sigma B) \longrightarrow R^{2}F(B)
\] 
of the circular sequence of the triangle $F(I^{1}), F(\Sigma^{2} B), Z^{2}$. Since 
$Z_{1} \longrightarrow R^{1}F(B)$ is epic, these two modules have the same image in 
$\overline{F}(\Sigma^{2} B)$, and this yields the desired result for the third row. The same argument applies to the remaining rows.

(2) The top part of~\eqref{D:circ-diag-extended} yields the commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 F(B) \ar[r] \ar[rd]
 & R^{0}F(B) \ar[d, tail] \ar[rd, "\iota \beta_{F}"] \ar[r, "\beta_{F}"]
 & \overline{F}(\Sigma B) \ar[d, "\iota", tail]
 \\
 & F(I^{0}) \ar[r]
 & F(\Sigma B)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
If $F$ is half-exact, the lower peripheral sequence is exact at $F(I^{0})$. By the parallelogram lemma, b), the top peripheral sequence is exact at $R^{0}F(B)$. Since $\iota$ is monic, the top row is also exact at that spot, which is the desired claim for $R^{0}F$.

To prove the exactness at $R^{1}F$, we examine the commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 F(\Sigma B) \ar[r] \ar[rd, "\eta \pi"] \ar[d, two heads, "\pi"']
 & Z_{1} \ar[d, two heads] \ar[rd]
 \\
 S^{1}F(B) \ar[r, "\eta"']
 & R^{1}F(B) \ar[r]
 & \overline{F}(\Sigma^{2} B)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The circular sequence for the composable pair $F(e_{1}), F(m_{1})$ produces 
a sequence 
\[
\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} F(e_{1}) \longrightarrow Z_{1} \longrightarrow \overline{F}(\Sigma^{2} B),
\]
which is exact at $Z_{1}$. If $F$ is half-exact, then $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} F(e_{1}) = \operatorname{\mathrm{Im}} F(m)$, which shows that the top peripheral sequence in the parallelogram above becomes exact at $Z_{1}$. By the parallelogram lemma, a), the lower peripheral sequence is exact at $R^{1}F(B)$. Since $\pi$  is epic, the bottom row is exact at the same spot, which is the desired claim for $R^{1}F$. The same argument applies to the remaining $R^{i}F$.

(3) If $F$ is epi-preserving, then $S^{1}F = 0$, and we are done by the exactness of the circular sequence of the diagram~\eqref{D:circ-diag} at $\overline{F}(\Sigma B)$.

(4) If $F$ is mono-preserving, then $\overline{F} = 0$, and we are done by (1).

(5) This is well-known.

label: C:connect-iso
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C:connect-iso}
If $F$ is a right-exact functor, then the canonical natural transformation $R^{i}F \longrightarrow \overline{F} \circ \Sigma^{i+1}$ is an isomorphism for each $i \geq 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $F$ is right-exact, $S^{i}F = 0$ for each $i \geq 1$. The result now follows from the exactness of the fundamental sequence.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Suppose $F$ is left-exact but not exact. Then the fundamental sequence is exact by~(2) and $\rho_{F}$ is an isomorphism by~(5). It follows that the converse of (3) is not true in general.

label: EG:tensor-product
title: Example
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Suppose $\Lambda$ is left hereditary. Then $R^{0}(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq I(A\otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$, the quotient functor of $A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $ by the largest subfunctor vanishing on injectives, and the sequence~\eqref{Eq: 4-term for tensor product} becomes
 \[
 0 \longrightarrow A \operatorname{\overset{\rightharpoondown}{\otimes}} \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \longrightarrow A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \longrightarrow I(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow  0.
 \]
 In particular, $I(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is an exact functor.\footnote{The functor $I(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is not as mysterious as it may seem. Without any assumption 
 on~$\Lambda$ or on $A$, its value on a left module $B$ can be computed by applying $A\otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $ to a cosyzygy sequence 
 $0 \to B \to I \to \Sigma B \to 0$ and taking the kernel of the induced map $A \otimes I \to A \otimes \Sigma B$.}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since the cosyzygy module of any module is injective, $A \operatorname{\overset{\rightharpoondown}{\otimes}} (\Sigma_{\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }) = 0$. Since the fundamental sequence is exact, we then have $R^{0}(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq I(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$. To show that  $I(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is exact, we first notice that it preserves epimorphisms because it is a quotient of the right-exact functor $A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $. Being a zeroth right-derived functor, it is also left-exact, and therefore exact.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: $w(F) := \operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} f$ is called the \texttt{defect} of $F$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
If $F$ is a finitely presented covariant functor, then 
 \[
 R^{i} \rho_{F} : R^{i}F \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{i}(w(F), \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )
 \]
is an isomorphism for all $i$. \qed
head: environment

label: D:Tr
title: Example
body_md:
We again set $F := A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $ and assume that $A$ is \texttt{finitely presented}, i.e., there is an exact sequence 
 \[
 P_{1} \overset{d}\longrightarrow P_{0} \overset{p}\longrightarrow A \longrightarrow 0,
 \]
with $P_{0}$ and $P_{1}$ finitely generated projectives. This sequence gives rise to an exact sequence of functors
 \[
 P_{1} \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \overset{d \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }\longrightarrow P_{0} \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \longrightarrow A\otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \longrightarrow 0,
 \]
which is isomorphic to the sequence
\[
 (P_{1}^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \overset{(d^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )}\longrightarrow (P_{0}^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \longrightarrow 0.
 \]
Thus $A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $ is finitely presented.
To compute its defect, we use the defining exact sequence for the transpose of $A$
\begin{equation}\label{D:Tr}
0 \longrightarrow A^{\ast} \overset{p^{\ast}}\longrightarrow P_{0}^{\ast} \overset{d^{\ast}}\longrightarrow P_{1}^{\ast} \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A \longrightarrow 0,
\end{equation}
which shows that $w(A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq A^{\ast}$. As a result, the exact sequence~\eqref{Eq: 4-term for tensor product} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{Eq:4-term-tensor-half-explicit}
\xymatrix
	{
	0 \ar[r]
	& A \operatorname{\overset{\rightharpoondown}{\otimes}} \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \ar[r]
	& A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \ar[r]^{\rho_{A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }}
	& (A^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]
	& A \operatorname{\overset{\rightharpoondown}{\otimes}} \Sigma \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \ar[r]
	& 0.
	}
\end{equation}
One can also check that $\rho_{A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }$ evaluates on a module $B$ according to the rule
\[
a \otimes b \mapsto l : f \mapsto f(a)b.
\]
To further explicate the structure of \eqref{Eq:4-term-tensor-half-explicit}, we compute $A \operatorname{\overset{\rightharpoondown}{\otimes}} \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $. The foregoing calculations produce a commutative diagram with an exact row
\[
\xymatrix
	{
	0 \ar[r]
	& (\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]
	& (P_{1}^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]^{(d^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )}
	& (P_{0}^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]^{\pi} \ar[rd]_{(p^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )}
	& A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \ar[r] \ar[d]^{\rho_{A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }}
	& 0
\\
	&
	&
	&
	& (A^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )
	}
\]
The circular sequence for the composable morphisms $\pi$ and $\rho_{A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }$ yields a short exact sequence 
\[
0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} \pi \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} (p^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow 
\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} \rho_{A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} } \longrightarrow 0
\]
Notice that $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} \pi = \operatorname{\mathrm{Im}} (d^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} \rho_{A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} } = A \operatorname{\overset{\rightharpoondown}{\otimes}} \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $. To identify the middle term, choose an epimorphism $q : Q \twoheadrightarrow A^{\ast}$ with $Q$ projective. This gives the first three terms of a projective resolution 
\begin{equation}
\ldots \longrightarrow Q \overset{p^{\ast}q}\longrightarrow P_{0}^{\ast} \overset{d^{\ast}}\longrightarrow P_{1}^{\ast} \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A \longrightarrow 0
\end{equation}
of  $\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A$, which is enough for computing $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$. Since $(q, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is monic, $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}}(p^{\ast}q, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) = \operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}}(p^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$, and we recover the well-known isomorphism.
\[
\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq \operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} (p^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )/\operatorname{\mathrm{Im}} (d^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq A \operatorname{\overset{\rightharpoondown}{\otimes}} \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} .
\]
Finally, using dimension shift on the covariant argument of $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}$, we rewrite~\eqref{Eq:4-term-tensor-half-explicit} in a more explicit form
\begin{equation}\label{Eq:4-term-tensor-explicit}
0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  
\overset{\rho_{A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{1.5mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }}\longrightarrow (A^{\ast}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow
\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{2}(\operatorname{\mathrm{Tr}} A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow 0,
\end{equation}
thus recovering Auslander's exact sequence~\eqref{D:ext}.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $\mathscr{T}$ be the class of injectively stable covariant functors and 
 $\mathscr{F}$ the class of mono-preserving covariant functors. Then 
 $(\mathscr{T}, \mathscr{F})$ is a hereditary torsion theory in the (large) category of additive covariant functors. \qed
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Returning to an arbitrary (i.e., not necessarily left-hereditary) ring, we  have, by~\cite[Proposition~4.3]{A66}, that defect-zero half-exact finitely presented functors  on the module category are precisely the injective objects in the category of defect-zero finitely presented functors. We also have [idem.] that such functors are precisely  direct summands of the functors $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(D, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$. It is interesting to revisit this result from a constructive point of view. Over a left hereditary ring, if we know a short exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$  which gives rise to a defining exact sequence for $F$, 
 \[
 0 \longrightarrow (C, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow (B, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow (A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow 0,
 \]
then~\cite[Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.3]{A66} show that we can set $D := C$. In general, we may ask if there is a ``coordinate-free'' description of $D$. For example, the foregoing argument and the universal coefficient formula for cohomology (see Section~\ref{S:ucfc} below) show that, for $F := \mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$, we can set 
\[
D:=  \mathrm{H}_{n-1}(\mathbf{C}) \simeq w(\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )).
\] 
While this formula may be viewed as being coordinate-free, it requires the use of a different functor, i.e.,  $\mathrm{H}_{n-1}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$.

Recall that a direct summand of a covariant $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}$ need not be an $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}$, as was shown by Auslander in~\cite{A69}, refuting an earlier conjecture of his own. The conjecture is, however, true if the domain category of $F$ has denumerable sums~\cite{Fr66}, or if it is of finite global dimension~\cite[Theorem~4.8]{A66}, or if the fixed argument of $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}$ is artinian (or, more generally, is noetherian and has the descending chain condition for the images of nested endomorphisms)~\cite[Proposition~11]{M-2016}. In those cases, $F \simeq \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(D, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$, and one may ask how to recover $D$ from the functor $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(D, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$.  As~$D$ is defined only up to projectively stable equivalence, one has to look for an answer in the stable category. In that category, the isomorphism type of $D$ is uniquely determined by the isomorphism type of the corresponding representable functor $(\underline{D, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} })$, and this immediately leads to the desired solution:
\[
(\underline{D, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }) \simeq S_{1}\operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(D, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq S_{1}F,\footnote{The reader who feels the given answer is not ``constructive'' enough for computational purposes may rethink what it means to compute and start thinking of computing with functors.}
\] 
where $S_{1}$ denotes the left satellite.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $\mathbf{C} : 
\ldots \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}_{n+1} \overset{d_{n+1}}\longrightarrow \mathrm{C}_{n} \overset{d_{n}}\longrightarrow \mathrm{C}_{n-1} \longrightarrow \ldots$ be an arbitrary complex. Then
 \[
w(\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )) \simeq \operatorname{\mathrm{Ker}} (\mathrm{C}_{n}/\mathrm{B}_{n} \to \mathrm{C}_{n-1}) \simeq \mathrm{H}_{n}(\mathbf{C}). 
\]
As a consequence, 
\[
R^{i}(\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )) \simeq \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{i}(\mathrm{H}_{n}(\mathbf{C}), \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )
\]
for all integers $i$. \qed
head: environment

label: D:rfs-co-arb
title: \thistheoremname
body_md:
{Universal Coefficient Theorem for Cohomology of Arbitrary Complexes}
 Let $\mathbf{C}$ be an arbitrary complex. Then the right fundamental sequence for $\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is of the form
\begin{equation}\label{D:rfs-co-arb}
\begin{tikzcd}
 0 \ar[r] 
   & \overline{\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }) \ar[r] 
      & \mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r] 
                  \ar[d, phantom, ""{coordinate, name=Z}]
         & (\mathrm{H}_{n}(\mathbf{C}), \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[dll, rounded corners,
                                   to path={ -- ([xshift=2ex]\tikztostart.east)
						|- (Z) [pos=0.3]\tikztonodes
						-| ([xshift=-2ex]\tikztotarget.west) 
						-- (\tikztotarget)}] 
\\
   & \overline{\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }) \circ \Sigma \ar[r] 
      & S^{1} (\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )) \ar[r]

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For a module $B$, choose an exact sequence $0 \to B \to I \to \Sigma B \to 0$ with an injective $I$, apply $F$, and pass to the corresponding long exact sequence.

label: L:stab=Ext
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L:stab=Ext}
 Suppose $\mathbf{C}$ is a projective complex. Then $(\mathrm{H}^{i}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ))_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a cohomological functor, and, for each integer $n$, the canonical natural transformation 
 \[
 \xi^{n-1} : \overline{\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }) \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\mathrm{C}_{n-1}/\mathrm{B}_{n-1},\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) 
 \]
 is an isomorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathbf{C}$ is projective, applying the functor $(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ to a short exact sequence of modules produces a short exact sequence of complexes. The first result now follows from the fact that cohomology is a cohomological functor on complexes.
 
 To prove the second assertion, apply the Yoneda embedding to the short exact sequence~\eqref{D:F-inj-stab}, pass to the cohomology long exact sequence, and compare the result with~\eqref{D:Fsub-res}.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Suppose $\mathbf{C}$ is a projective complex. Then the natural transformation  
 $\theta^{n} : S^{1}(\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )) \longrightarrow \overline{\mathrm{H}^{n+1}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} })$ induced by $\delta^{n}$ is a functor isomorphism. The composition
 \[
 \xi^{n}\theta^{n} : S^{1}(\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )) \longrightarrow 
 \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\mathrm{C}_{n}/\mathrm{B}_{n},\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )
 \] 
 is an isomorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma~\ref{L:stab=Ext}, $(\mathrm{H}^{i}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ))_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a cohomological functor. The first assertion is then a consequence of Lemma~\ref{L:S=stab}. The second assertion follows from Lemma~\ref{L:stab=Ext}.

{Universal Coefficient Theorem for Cohomology of Projective Complexes}
  Let $\mathbf{C}$ be a projective complex. Then the right fundamental sequence for $\mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is exact and of the form

\begin{tikzcd}[cramped, sep=small]
 0 \ar[r] 
   & \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\mathrm{C}_{n-1}/\mathrm{B}_{n-1},\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r] 
      & \mathrm{H}^{n}(\mathbf{C}, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r] 
                  \ar[d, phantom, ""{coordinate, name=Z}]
         & (\mathrm{H}_{n}(\mathbf{C}), \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[dll, rounded corners,
                                   to path={ -- ([xshift=2ex]\tikztostart.east)
						|- (Z) [pos=0.3]\tikztonodes
						-| ([xshift=-2ex]\tikztotarget.west) 
						-- (\tikztotarget)}] 
\\
   & \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{2}(\mathrm{C}_{n-1}/\mathrm{B}_{n-1},\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r] 
      & \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\mathrm{C}_{n}/\mathrm{B}_{n},\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]
      			  \ar[d, phantom, ""{coordinate, name=Y}]
         & \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{1}(\mathrm{H}_{n}(\mathbf{C}), \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[dll, rounded corners,
                                   to path={ -- ([xshift=2ex]\tikztostart.east)
						|- (Y) [near end]\tikztonodes
						-| ([xshift=-2ex]\tikztotarget.west) 
						-- (\tikztotarget)}] 
\\
   & \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{3}(\mathrm{C}_{n-1}/\mathrm{B}_{n-1},\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r] 
      & \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{2}(\mathrm{C}_{n}/\mathrm{B}_{n},\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )  \ar[r]

\\

head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Assume $\mathscr{A}$ is the category of left $\Lambda$-modules over a ring 
 $\Lambda$. Recall that the canonical natural transformation $F(\Lambda) \otimes _{\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} } \longrightarrow F$ is an isomorphism on~$\Lambda$. If $F$ preserves direct sums, then this transformation is an isomorphism on all projectives, and therefore it is isomorphic to the zeroth left-derived transformation for $F$. In particular, $L_{i}F \simeq \operatorname{\mathrm{Tor}}_{i}(F(\Lambda), \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ for all $i$.
head: environment

label: E:co-4-term for hom
title: Example
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Suppose $\Lambda$ is left hereditary. Then $L_{0}(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq P(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$, the functor of maps with domain $A$ factoring through projectives, and the sequence~\eqref{E:co-4-term for hom}  becomes
 \[
 \xymatrix
	{
	0 \ar[r]        
	& P(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]^{\lambda_{A}}
	& (A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \ar[r]
	& (\underline{A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} }) \ar[r]
	& 0.
	}
 \]
 In particular, $P(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is an exact functor.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the syzygy module of any module is projective, the first term of the fundamental sequence vanishes. Since the fundamental sequence is exact, we also
 have $L_{0}(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ) \simeq P(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$. To show that $P(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$ is exact, we first notice that it preserves monomorphisms because it is a subfunctor of the left-exact functor $(A, \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} )$. Being a zeroth left-derived functor, it is also right-exact, and therefore exact.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
An additive functor from (left) $\Lambda$-modules to abelian groups is said to be tensor-copresented (\textrm{TC}, for short) if it is isomorphic to the kernel of a natural transformation between univariate tensor product functors. In other words, $F$ is TC if it is defined by an exact sequence
 \[
 0 \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \longrightarrow B \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} ,
 \]
 where $A$ and $B$ are right $\Lambda$-modules.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The reader who is familiar with the Auslander-Gruson-Jensen (AGJ) duality, will immediately see that TC functors on left modules are precisely the AGJ transforms of finitely presented functors on right modules.\footnote{The functor $A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $ is not in general an injective object in a functor category. Indeed, suppose the ring $\Lambda$ is von Neumann regular but not semisimple. Then there is a nonsplit  exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$, and it must be pure. Apply the tensor embedding to get a short exact sequence of functors $0 \to A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \to B \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}   \to C \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}   \to 0$ (because the original sequence is pure exact). If $A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $ were injective, then this sequence would split, which would imply that the original sequence is split, too, a contradiction.

Now we can also show that the AGJ transformation is not always exact on tensor-copresented functors. Start with the same sequence as before and apply the tensor embedding to get a short exact sequence in the functor category. Now assume the AGJ transformation is exact and apply it to the obtained sequence. Get a short exact sequence of representable functors. It must split because representables are projective. Now applying the AGJ transformation again, we have the split exact sequence of tensor product functors we started with. But then the original sequence must split, a contradiction.}
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $A$ be a right module and $G$ an additive functor from left modules to abelian groups. If $G$ preserves direct sums, then any natural transformation $\phi : A \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm}  \longrightarrow G$ is uniquely determined by its $\prescript{}{\Lambda}\Lambda$-component.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It follows from the assumptions that $\phi$ is uniquely determined on free left modules. To see that the same is true for any left module $X$, take a free presentation of $X$, apply $\phi$, and use the naturality of $\phi$ together with the fact that the tensor product is right-exact.

body_md: The maps $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are inverses of each other. \qed

title: Theorem
body_md: In the above diagram, $K \simeq \underline{F}$ and the bottom row is a tensor copresentation of $\underline{F}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We only need to prove the first assertion. We view the first three columns and the maps between them as a short exact sequence of complexes. Since the third column is exact, the map between the first two is a quasi-isomorphism (i.e., induces an isomorphism on the homology). In particular, the first column is exact at $F$ and $p = \operatorname{\mathrm{coker}} \lambda_{F}$. Furthermore, $\lambda_{F}$ is clearly an isomorphism on projectives. Together with the fact that  $K_{f} \otimes \hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} $ is right-exact, it shows that $\lambda_{F}$ is the zeroth left-derived transformation for $F$, and therefore $K$ is the quot-stabilization of $F$.

body_md:
If $F$ is a right-exact functor, then the canonical natural transformation 
 $R_{i}F \longrightarrow \overline{F} \circ \Omega^{i+1}$ is an isomorphism for each $i \geq 1$. \qed

title: Remark
body_md:
Assume $\mathscr{A}$ is the category of left $\Lambda$-modules over a ring 
 $\Lambda$. Recall that for any contravariant functor $F$, the canonical natural transformation $ F \to \big(\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} , F(\Lambda)\big)$ is an isomorphism on $\Lambda$. If $F$ carries coproducts to products, then this natural transformation is an isomorphism on all projectives, and therefore it is isomorphic to~$\rho_{F}$. Hence, the canonical natural transformation 
\[
R_{i}\rho_{F} : R_{i}F \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{i}(\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} , F(\Lambda))
\] 
is an isomorphism for all $i$, and each row of~\eqref{D:rfs-contra-fun} rewrites as 
\[
\overline{F} \circ \Omega^{i} \longrightarrow S^{i}F \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{i}(\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} , F(\Lambda)).
\]
Recall also that if $F$ is finitely presented, then the covariant defect $v(F)$ 
of~$F$ is defined as $F(\Lambda)$. If a finite presentation of $F$ arises as the Yoneda embedding of $f : B \longrightarrow A$, then $v(F) \simeq \operatorname{\mathrm{Coker}} f \simeq F(\Lambda)$, and each row of the left fundamental sequence is of the form
\[
\overline{F} \circ \Omega^{i} \longrightarrow S^{i}F \longrightarrow \operatorname{\mathrm{Ext}}^{i}(\hspace{0.04cm} \rule{2.4mm}{.4pt} \hspace{0.04cm} , v(F)).
\]

title: Corollary
body_md:
Suppose $F$ is a left-exact functor. Then the canonical natural transformation  
 $\underline{F} \circ \Sigma^{i+1} \longrightarrow  L^{i}F $ is an isomorphism for each $i \geq 1$.  \qed

There is a functor isomorphism $h_{J} \circ \overline{F} \simeq \overline{h}_{G(J)}$.
\qed
